Beyond RoboMME (Sec. 7) J: MIKASA-Robo, exploratory

Appendix A Protocol and statistics

Episodes.

Every cell uses the 50 test episodes of RoboMME for the task, with the benchmark’s environment seeds and policy noise seed 7, so that all conditions of a model are paired episode by episode. The required number of repetitions KK is set by the benchmark: on PickXtimes 16, 10, 12, 6 and 6 episodes have K=1,…,5K=1,\dots,5; on SwingXtimes 15, 12 and 23 episodes have K=1,2,3K=1,2,3. Held-out confirmations use the benchmark’s 50 validation episodes per task (other environment seeds, same difficulty mix).

Null events.

Events are injected at action-chunk boundaries after policy steps 48 and 160 (other times in Appendix B). During a pause the robot holds its last joint target and the policy is not queried; during a fidget the wrist rolls ±0.3\pm 0.3 rad around the held target; an air-grasp is executed by the motion planner above a resting object and returns to the pre-event pose. After each event the evaluator checks and logs that no object moved by more than 1 cm and no button was pressed. On tasks whose scene draws fading highlights (gripper trail, button glow), the highlight clock is frozen during the pause so that the images after the pause match those before it; on RouteStick, the evaluator’s gripper trace is not extended during the pause. In the hidden condition, the event is executed identically but its frames are not written to memory and the time stamps do not advance over it. Figure 9 shows a fidget and an air-grasp frame by frame.

Failure classes.

From the end-of-episode record we classify a failure as early (the policy pressed the button or submitted at a stage before the KK-th repetition was complete), extra (it failed at or after the stopping stage, or timed out, having completed KK repetitions), or other. Some runs of the released model predate stage logging; their failures are listed as unclassified (Uncl.) and are not used for any statement about failure direction, unless a stage-logged rerun reproduces the cell episode by episode (Appendix B).

Tests.

All comparisons are paired on episodes and use the exact two-sided McNemar test on the discordant pairs. Appendix L lists every cell of the four models analysed throughout (released FrameSamp-Modul, Clock, Clock with the event index, NoClock) with Wilson 95% intervals and Holm-corrected pp-values over these 42 comparisons; every effect there that the main text calls significant remains significant after correction. Appendices E and I use a broader core family of 59 pre-specified tests (rescaling, route split, designs, event index) and state which effects survive it. Where a test was pre-registered, the prediction and its rule were logged before the run; Appendix K lists them with their outcomes.

Training variance and a second machine.

Each from-scratch model was trained with seed 42; Clock and NoClock were also trained with seed 43 (below). Two further training runs of the Clock recipe with the same seed, which differ only through GPU non-determinism, and one on a second machine bound the training-level variation (Tab. 4): the pause damage reproduces within 2 episodes, whereas the no-event and hidden cells on PickXtimes vary by up to 12 and 9 episodes. Intermediate checkpoints of rerun 1 also show that the reliance on the clock grows with the ability to count: from 10k to 30k training steps, success without events rises from 28 to 44 on PickXtimes, while success with time stamps scaled by 1.5 stays at 23–27, and failures under a 0.5 scale turn from early stops into extra repetitions. The pause-augmentation model and its control are trained and evaluated on a second machine (H200 GPUs of a different variant, different driver and CPU). Running the released model there reproduces the cluster’s results within 3 episodes (PickXtimes 44 against 47, SwingXtimes 46 against 44) with 95 of 100 episodes agreeing.

A second training seed.

We trained Clock and NoClock again with seed 43, on the second machine, with the recipe unchanged, and compare them with each other (same seed, same machine). Rules, written before training: NoClock counts as well (no event at least that of Clock − 6-\,6, both tasks); it does not read the stamps (×1.5\times 1.5 at least its own no event − 6-\,6, PickXtimes); pauses still hurt it (visible at most its own hidden − 8-\,8, both tasks); pauses hurt Clock (visible at most its own no event − 15-\,15, both tasks); a fast clock causes early stops in Clock (×1.5\times 1.5 at most its own no event − 10-\,10, at least 75% of failures early). A miss would be reported and the claim narrowed. All five hold (Tab. 5): NoClock 39 and 47 against Clock 37 and 44; ×1.5\times 1.5 38 against 39; visible 24 and 15 against hidden 38 and 43; Clock 37 to 17 and 44 to 15; Clock ×1.5\times 1.5 27 against 37 (−11/+1-11/{+}1, p=.006p{=}.006), 22 of 23 failures early, at the threshold. Not registered: on SwingXtimes, among episodes that succeed without the event and stop early with it, NoClock’s presses with K=3K{=}3 under pauses come after two swings in 5 of 8 (2 after one), Clock’s after one in 10 of 12, a contrast in the same direction as with seed 42 (14 of 14 and 19 of 21) but less clean. Counting all early presses: 6 of 9 and 10 of 14 (seed 42: 17 of 17 and 21 of 23); presses after one, 2 of 9 against 10 of 14, Fisher p=.04p{=}.04.

Appendix B Robustness of the phenomenon

The early stops of Sec. 4 do not hinge on one length, time or kind of stop: the damage sets in once a pause lasts 0.5–1.5 s, appears wherever a decision to stop still lies ahead, and follows from many short random stops as well. Where a fidget nudges a held cube, the damage is the same as where it moves nothing; the one event that interferes with the task, the air-grasp on PickXtimes, is excluded from the main text.

Table 6 varies how long the null event lasts, when it happens, and whether it is one designed event or many short, randomly timed stops. All cells use the released FrameSamp-Modul and are paired with the same 50 episodes without an event. Failure classes for the 5-second pauses come from a rerun with stage logging that reproduces the cell episode by episode (16 and 10 successes; no episode changes outcome): 34 of 34 failures on PickXtimes and 36 of 40 on SwingXtimes are early.

Dose.

The damage sets in between 0.5 and 1.5 s per pause and saturates by 5 s: two 15-second pauses do no more harm than two 5-second ones, and hiding either restores success. Saturation is expected if the policy stops at the first decision point after its estimate of progress overshoots; a longer pause cannot make it stop earlier than that.

Timing.

A single pause hurts wherever it falls, but only in episodes that still have a decision to make after it. With the pause at step 48, K=1K=1 episodes are untouched (16 of 16 on PickXtimes), whereas only 2 of 34 episodes with K≥2K\geq 2 succeed. With the pause at step 300, PickXtimes episodes with K≤2K\leq 2, which are nearly finished by then, are untouched (25 of 26), whereas those with K≥3K\geq 3 fail (1 of 24). This rules out an immediate reflex to stop after any pause and matches a stop decision taken when the remembered elapsed time reaches its usual value.

Natural stops.

Many short stops at random times, as a safety layer or a slow planner might produce, are nearly as harmful as two long pauses, and again only through memory: hidden, they leave success at the no-event level. They are also a boundary of the event index (Appendix I).

The PickXtimes air-grasp.

On PickXtimes the air-grasp that returns to its starting pose leaves 12 of 50 (43 hidden), but its failures do not have the clock signature: they concentrate at K=1K=1 (2 of 16 succeed, against 16 of 16 for every other event), where no early stop is possible. The second air-grasp often happens just after the cube has been released, and the returning open gripper encloses the cube; the policy then grasps it again. The event is therefore not null on this task and is excluded from the main text; on SwingXtimes the same event behaves as the other null events.

Null-event validity.

Every fidget and air-grasp is logged with the largest object displacement and the button state; a pause holds the current joint targets, toward which the arm keeps settling for a median of 14 (PickXtimes) and 16 (SwingXtimes) steps, at most 23, after which no arm joint moves by more than 10−510^{-5} rad per step (Sec. B.1). The policies do not pause on their own: in 850 rollouts without injected events (PickXtimes and SwingXtimes), the arm never stays below 10−410^{-4} rad per step for more than 2 consecutive steps, so every null event studied here is injected. Air-grasps moved an object by more than 1 cm in at most 8 of 50 SwingXtimes episodes (none on PickXtimes). A wrist fidget performed while a cube is held can nudge it beyond 1 cm: in 17–33 of 50 episodes per cell, at similar rates with the frames visible and hidden, because the physical event is the same. We keep these episodes, since the paired comparison holds the physical event fixed. Table 7 shows that the damage does not depend on them.

B.1 Hiding a pause only once the arm is still

On SwingXtimes, hiding a pause does not fully restore Clock (38 against 48 without an event) or LTM-π\pi (31 against 50; Sec. G.2). The hidden condition drops every frame of the hold, including the arm’s settling motion at its start, which on SwingXtimes interrupts carrying the cube. Prediction fixed before the run: if dropping that motion explains the gap, a condition that sends the hold frames while the arm still moves and hides the rest should reach at least the no-event success minus 3 on SwingXtimes for both models (Clock ≥45\geq 45, LTM-π\pi ≥47\geq 47), and match the hidden condition on PickXtimes. The arm counts as still from the first frame at which no arm joint moves by 10−510^{-5} rad and neither finger by 10−510^{-5} m; the threshold, about twice the largest per-step change of a settled arm and below every step of 430 k steps of normal motion, was set from existing joint logs before the run. It keeps 5–16 of the 100 frames of each hold.

The prediction fails for both models: on SwingXtimes success reaches 27 (Clock) and 34 (LTM-π\pi), on PickXtimes it matches the hidden condition (37 and 49). The settling frames are thus not what the hidden condition is missing; sending them instead turns failures towards early presses (Clock 17 of 23, LTM-π\pi 11 of 16), as if a few frames of a still interval were already read as progress. What else separates hidden pauses from no event on SwingXtimes for these two models is open, so all their SwingXtimes comparisons are made against no event, where the visible damage is larger still.

Appendix C Null events across all 16 RoboMME tasks

Table 9 applies the protocol of Sec. 4 to every RoboMME task: released FrameSamp-Modul, two 15-second pauses (300 steps, after policy steps 48 and 160), visible or hidden, 50 paired episodes per cell. Two tasks at floor were not run; tasks with fewer than 15 no-event successes are reported but not interpreted (rule fixed before the runs).

Counting tasks: through the clock.

PickXtimes and SwingXtimes are analysed in Secs. 5.2 and 5.3. BinFill, which also ends with a button press, behaves the same: 9 visible against 21 hidden. Advancing only the time stamps over the pause reproduces the damage (time only 7 against 23 without an event, −16/+0-16/{+0}, p<10−4p<10^{-4}); storing only the null frames does not significantly change success (content only 19, −5/+1-5/{+1}, p=.22p{=}.22). Rescaling all time stamps does not significantly change BinFill (23 to 18 at ×0.5\times 0.5, p=.23p{=}.23; 23 at ×1.5\times 1.5), so here the role of the clock rests on the pause decomposition alone.

Video-conditioned tasks: through eviction of the video.

Nine tasks open with a demonstration video sampled into the same 32 uniformly spaced slots as the execution frames, so a visible pause pushes video frames out of memory (RouteStick: from about 24 slots to about 10). Starvation injects no pause but gives the video only the slots it keeps under the visible pause; protection injects the visible pause but keeps the video’s no-event slot count. Starvation reproduces the visible damage and protection restores the hidden level (starved and protected against visible and hidden): RouteStick 4 and 32 against 7 and 36; PatternLock 19 and 28 against 19 and 28; VideoPlaceButton 14 and 27 against 11 and 29. Starved never differs significantly from visible (p≥.37p\geq.37), nor protected from hidden (p≥.29p\geq.29); protection beats the visible pause on every task (p≤.012p\leq.012). The time stamps play no measurable role here: protection restores success although the stamps still advance over the pause, and on RouteStick rescaling them leaves success unchanged (33 at ×0.5\times 0.5, 35 at ×1.5\times 1.5, against 33). On MoveCube the drop under eviction is small and not significant (33 against 39 hidden, p=.15p{=}.15). Of the remaining tasks, two meet the 15-success threshold besides StopCube, and the pre-registered prediction misses on both. Harm was predicted to be largest where key information is shown only briefly at the start, and to shrink with video length; instead the short-video VideoUnmask loses only 3 (16 against 19, p=.25p{=}.25), and the long-video VideoPlaceOrder 6 (15 against 21, p=.11p{=}.11), neither significant. A post hoc reading: a pause can only take away what memory contributes, and on these two tasks the released policy barely beats the same backbone without memory (π0.5\pi_{0.5}: 14 and 14, against 17 and 18). Where memory matters most, VideoRepick (π0.5\pi_{0.5}: 0 of 50), the visible pause cuts success from 15 to 5 (p=.002p{=}.002), but this task is below the threshold and is reported only.

StopCube: time is the task.

In StopCube elapsed time is legitimate information: in 98 of 100 demonstrations the robot hovers still above the button, for a median of 198 steps, before pressing. Rescaling the time stamps in either direction lowers success from 24 to 6 (×0.5\times 0.5, −23/+5-23/{+5}, p<10−3p<10^{-3}) and 5 (×1.5\times 1.5, −22/+3-22/{+3}, p<10−3p<10^{-3}). Because hiding a pause also removes real elapsed time, our prediction, recorded before the run, is the reverse of the other tasks: hiding should not help, and may hurt. The prediction holds only trivially: both conditions collapse (2 visible, 0 hidden, against 24 without an event), so the comparison is at floor and we do not interpret it; whatever the memory does, a 15-second interruption leaves StopCube nearly unsolvable.

Appendix D Time predicts progress in demonstrations

In scripted simulation and in real teleoperation alike, the time step alone predicts how many repetitions a demonstration has completed. This section defines the predictor, lists the data and bounds what the evidence shows.

Predictor.

At each step tt from the first repetition through the stop decision, the label is the number of repetitions completed by tt. The predictor sees only tt and outputs the most frequent training-fold label in the same 10-step bin (the overall most frequent label for unseen bins); neither KK nor the task is given. Accuracy uses 5-fold cross-validation over demonstrations; the baseline predicts the most frequent label. On RoboMME, repetition boundaries come from the recorded sub-goal text; on real data, a gripper cycle (flips under 0.25 s removed; a closure of at least 0.5 s followed by a release; the window ends at the last release). On RoboMME the two definitions agree (gripper-cycle count equals KK in 100 of 100 PickXtimes demonstrations; accuracy 0.894 against 0.890). Bins aligned to ≈\approx14 per stage instead of 10 frames give results within 0.006.

Pacing and idle stretches.

Within a task and stage, the coefficient of variation of stage durations is 0.11–0.13 in the real datasets and 0.08–0.13 on RoboMME. End-effector stillness (<0.5<0.5 mm per frame) of at least 2 s occurs in 0% (austin_sailor), 1.8% (stanford_hydra) and 1.1% (LIBERO-10) of demonstrations; 1 of 100 RoboMME PickXtimes demonstrations contains a still stretch (12 steps). FMB has one ≈\approx1.5 s hold per demonstration, always at the same phase (grasp settling), so it is part of the regular pace.

Scope of this evidence.

The correlation the shortcut exploits is as strong in regular (three-cycle) real teleoperation demonstrations as in RoboMME, and weaker across all tasks (62% on stanford_hydra, 75% on FMB); this does not show that a policy trained on real data uses it, nor that a real robot fails under null events: all causal evidence in this paper comes from simulation. The real datasets are small (e.g. 30 demonstrations per task in austin_sailor), and public versions may have had idle frames trimmed during conversion, making them look more regular than raw collection; the statistics describe the data that VLA training actually consumes.

Appendix E The clock route in detail

A time-stamped policy reads a null event partly through its stamps. On PickXtimes, advancing the stamps over a pause of 5 s or more without storing its frames reproduces the full damage, rescaling them flips the failure even when their layout stays in distribution, and where the stamps carry the null interval and the two accounts of the press differ, presses follow the clock.

All manipulations are applied at test time to the released policies (FrameSamp-Modul unless noted); 50 paired episodes per cell, exact two-sided McNemar test against the same model without event. Two null events of LL steps follow policy steps 48 and 160 (Sec. 3); L=30,100,300L{=}30,100,300 is 1.5, 5 and 15 s. Failure types: e early (press before the KK-th repetition); x extra (failure after KK repetitions or time-out, as in Appendix A, and on SwingXtimes also a put-down failure without a press, which the tables of Appendix L list as other); u unclassified (no stage log).

E.1 Splitting a null event into frames and time stamps

A null event puts its frames into the 32 slots and advances the time stamps of all later frames. In all four conditions the robot pauses physically. Visible: null frames stored, stamps advance. Time only: null frames withheld, stamps as in visible. Content only: null frames stored with the last working stamp. Hidden: null frames withheld, stamps equal work time. Content only is not stamp-clean: at L=300L{=}300 about half of the slots share two repeated stamps and working frames are 2.4×\times further apart in stamp than normal, a layout never seen in training.

On Pick the stamps alone reproduce the full damage at L=100L{=}100 and 300300 (17 and 14 against 16; for FrameSamp-Expert 4 against 14), the frames alone part of it; at L=30L{=}30 each channel does about half. On Swing the damage at L=30L{=}30 goes entirely through the frames; at L=100L{=}100 and 300300 neither channel alone reaches the visible damage, so the two add up.

E.2 In-distribution manipulations of the clock

Graded rescaling.

Table 12 extends Fig. 4 to all scales we ran (stamps of all memory frames multiplied by ss; no event, no frame dropped). FrameSamp-Expert, which reads the same memory through a different pathway, flips the same way on PickXtimes: under ×0.5\times 0.5 its failures are mostly extra repetitions (14 of 16), under ×1.5\times 1.5 almost all early presses (17 of 18; Tab. 13).

On Pick a slower clock causes extra repetitions and a faster one early presses (flip ×\times0.5 vs ×\times1.5: 23 x/3 e against 0 x/32 e, Fisher p<10−4p<10^{-4}). ×\times0.5 keeps every stamp inside the training range, so this is not an extrapolation artefact. The effect is asymmetric: ×\times0.75 is harmless, ×\times1.1 is not, with its early presses at large KK (K=2K{=}2: 1 of 10; K=3K{=}3: 5/12; K=4K{=}4: 2/6; K=5K{=}5: 4/6), as expected if the policy presses once the clock passes a threshold near its usual press time.

Frozen clock.

Once 32 frames are stored, we overwrite their stamps with linspace⁡(0,T,32)\mathrm{linspace}(0,T,32), the layout of a training episode of length TT, whatever the true step. The stamp pattern is then in distribution, but the clock always reads about T/139T/139 repetitions on Pick (139 steps per repetition). A policy that counts by the clock should press early when KK is below this reading and repeat too often when KK is above it; it does (Tab. 14). On Swing the totals are 20, 32 and 17 at T=150,300,600T{=}150,300,600, with the same flips.

E.3 When does the policy press?

Definition.

We take the episodes that succeed without the event and fail early with it. With t0t_{0} the press step in the no-event run of the same episode, tt the press step with the event (null steps excluded) and nnull=2​Ln_{\text{null}}{=}2L, the work ratio is t/t0t/t_{0} and the elapsed ratio (t+nnull)/t0(t+n_{\text{null}})/t_{0}. Clock: the policy presses when elapsed time reaches its usual press time (elapsed ratio ≈1{\approx}1, somewhat below if the threshold lies below the usual press time, as ×\times1.1 suggests). Skip one: the null events of an episode together count as one repetition whatever their duration (work ratio ≈(K−1)/K{\approx}(K{-}1)/K, elapsed ratio ≈(K−1)/K+nnull/t0{\approx}(K{-}1)/K+n_{\text{null}}/t_{0}). A press can only follow a completed repetition, so both also predict the repetitions jj completed at the press: skip one j=K−1j{=}K{-}1; clock the first jj with t¯0​(j)+nnull≥t¯0​(K)\bar{t}_{0}(j)+n_{\text{null}}\geq\bar{t}_{0}(K), where t¯0​(j)\bar{t}_{0}(j) is the median no-event press time for jj repetitions (Pick: 279, 424, 579, 729, 852 steps for j=1..5j{=}1..5).

At L=100L{=}100 the two accounts nearly coincide.

Table 15 gives the ratios of Fig. 10 by KK. On Pick, skip one predicts 0.97–1.04 at every KK, as does the clock. At K=2K{=}2 an early press can only follow the first repetition, which fixes the elapsed ratio at (t¯0​(1)+200)/t¯0​(2)≈1.13(\bar{t}_{0}(1)+200)/\bar{t}_{0}(2)\approx 1.13 under any account. Written with the measured press times, skip one predicts 1.13, 1.08, 1.07, 1.09 for K=2..5K{=}2..5, as close to the data as the clock at K=2,3K{=}2,3 and further only at K=4,5K{=}4,5 (n=2n{=}2–6). The L=100L{=}100 ratios on Pick thus do not discriminate between the accounts.

Where the accounts differ, the stamps follow the clock.

With 600 null steps on Pick, or 200 on Swing (a swing takes 70–100 steps), the clock is past the usual press time at the first decision and predicts a press after the first repetition for every KK, whereas skip one predicts K−1K{-}1. Table 16 lists every stage-logged cell where the predictions differ (jj read from the end-of-episode sub-goal). Where the stamps carry the null interval (visible, fidget or time only on a time-stamped model), presses come at or before the clock prediction in 95 of 107 episodes; the exception is FrameSamp-Modul time only on Swing (4 of 9). Where only the frames carry it (content only on the released model; NoClock, Sec. F.4), presses on Swing skip exactly one repetition (17 of 20) and on Pick fall between the two predictions.

On the released FrameSamp-Modul at L=300L{=}300, which has no stage log, the median step of the failure (on Pick a press in 1486 of 1490 stage-logged cases) is 268–346 at every K=2..5K{=}2..5 for visible and time-only pauses, near one repetition (279) rather than K−1K{-}1 (579, 729 for K=4,5K{=}4,5); this reading is post hoc. At L=30L{=}30, where the null interval is much shorter than a repetition, the early presses on Pick also come after K−1K{-}1 repetitions (time only: 14 of 14 for K≥2K\geq 2; post hoc). The clock account explains this only if the press threshold lies well before the usual press time, as the ×1.1\times 1.1 rescaling also implies: it advances the clock at the decision after two repetitions by only about 40 steps, yet causes early presses there (5 of 5 for K=3K{=}3). The pre-registered dose test below decides between the two accounts.

Dose test on Clock (pre-registered).

Clock runs on both tasks with L=30L{=}30 and 300300, analysed as in Tab. 15. Criteria fixed before the run: clock if the median elapsed ratio at L=30L{=}30 lies in 0.85–1.20 and the median work ratio at L=300L{=}300 is ≤0.55\leq 0.55; skip one if the median elapsed ratio is <0.85<0.85 at L=30L{=}30 and ≥1.5\geq 1.5 at L=300L{=}300, with a work ratio near (K−1)/K(K{-}1)/K. Support requires both doses on the clock side; one each is partial; cells with fewer than 8 early failures are not interpreted.

By the registered rule the result is partial (Tab. 17): at L=30L{=}30 both tasks fall on the clock side (elapsed 0.88 and 0.99), but at L=300L{=}300 the work ratio misses the clock criterion (0.57 and 0.66) and matches the skip-one ratios. We did not foresee that the ratios cannot separate the two accounts at L=300L{=}300: no press can occur during a pause, and a 300-step pause outlasts the remaining work, so both accounts predict elapsed ratios well above 1; and the earliest press the clock account allows, after finishing the repetition in progress, lies above a work ratio of 0.55. The repetitions completed before the press do separate them when K≥3K{\geq}3 (clock: at most one, since the clock has passed the usual press time by the end of the second pause; skip one: K−1K{-}1). 34 of 36 such presses come after at most one repetition (all 21 on SwingXtimes), and 2 after K−1K{-}1; NoClock under the shorter pause, by contrast, presses after K−1K{-}1 swings in all 14 cases (Sec. F.4). At L=30L{=}30 both accounts allow K−1K{-}1, which is what we see (20 of 23), so this dose does not discriminate (see the L=30L{=}30 paragraph above). Because the repetition count was not the registered criterion, we repeat the test on held-out validation episodes with it as the only criterion, fixed before the run (clock if at least 75% of presses with K≥3K{\geq}3 come after at most one repetition, skip one if at least 75% come after K−1K{-}1). On held-out episodes the outcome is clock: all 29 presses with K≥3K{\geq}3 come after one repetition (PickXtimes 15, SwingXtimes 14), none after K−1K{-}1 (no-event success 38 and 44, with 2×3002{\times}300 pauses 10 and 14; 40 of 40 and 31 of 36 failures early).

E.4 Further controls

Hidden null events (the robot still pauses) leave Pick at 43–46 and Swing at 45–47, against 47 and 44 (all n.s.): the damage is not physical. A single 100-step pause harms only where a stop decision follows it: after step 48, 16 of 16 K=1K{=}1 episodes succeed; after step 300, 9 of 10 K=2K{=}2 but 0 of 12 K=3K{=}3. Two 10-step pauses leave 43 and 45 (n.s.).

Appendix F What a model without time stamps makes of a null event

Without time stamps, a pause still hurts through the slots it fills. The damage needs the null frames in memory but not what they show, grows with the number of null slots, and keeps the signature of early presses.

This section details the controls behind Sec. 5.3. Clock and NoClock are trained from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} base checkpoint for 30k steps with the released recipe; their configurations differ in one line (use_pos_emb). Tests and failure types are as in Appendix E.

F.1 What NoClock can see: slot order, not time stamps

The memory has 32 slots of 16 tokens. Slot jj holds stored frame ⌊j​t/31⌋\lfloor jt/31\rfloor, where tt is the newest stored frame; before step 32 the memory is shorter and padded on the right, in training and at test time. Each token is encoded as Linear⁡([image token;silu⁡(Wp​τ)])\mathrm{Linear}([\,\text{image token};\ \mathrm{silu}(W_{p}\,\tau)\,]), where τ\tau is the sinusoidal encoding of the frame’s time step; NoClock drops the τ\tau branch. The action expert reads memory through cross-attention with rotary position embeddings on both sides: memory keys get positions 0,…,5110,\dots,511 in slot order, action queries 512,…512,\dots; masked tokens leave the softmax without shifting the others’ positions. Both models thus know slot order, but under uniform sampling order carries no absolute time (slot jj is step j​t/31jt/31 for any tt). Without τ\tau, elapsed time is available only through the frames themselves: how much the scene changes between neighbouring slots, and how many slots show a still scene.

F.2 Slot layouts of the controls

Null swap keeps the number, position and stillness of the null slots and changes what they show. Duplicate fill shows the same real frames, with the same spacing, as the visible pause, but no null frames.

F.3 Results

Paired contrasts.

NoClock ignores the stamps: ×1.5\times 1.5 gives 44 vs 42 (p=.62p{=}.62), and keeping the null frames but setting the stamps to working time gives 22 vs 21 visible. What the null frames show does not matter: null swap vs visible, Pick 17 vs 21 (−7/+3-7/{+}3, p=.34p{=}.34), Swing 13 vs 14 (−4/+3-4/{+}3, p=1p{=}1); both remain far below hidden (−27/+0-27/{+}0 and −33/+0-33/{+}0). Sparser real history is harmless when the memory is full: duplicate fill does not differ from no event on either model (p≥.29p\geq.29).

F.4 When NoClock presses

After a visible pause on Pick, NoClock presses at 0.74 of its usual working steps and 1.13 of its usual elapsed time. This does not show that it reads elapsed time: at L=100L{=}100 on Pick the clock and skip-one accounts predict the same repetition count (Sec. E.3), and NoClock matches both. Where the two differ, NoClock follows skip one: on Swing K=3K{=}3 it presses after two swings in 14 of 14 episodes (16 of 18 with null swap), where the clock account predicts one and Clock presses after one in 19 of 21; with a second training seed the same contrast is weaker (NoClock 5 of 8 after two, Clock 10 of 12 after one, same selection; Appendix A). To see how much one interval counts for, we ran one 5-second pause after step 48 with outcomes fixed in advance: one pause alone reads as about one repetition if on Swing at least 8 early presses with K=3K{=}3 occur and at least 75% come after two swings; only the pair does if success stays within 6 of no event or fewer than 8 such presses occur. All 10 come after two swings (all K=3K{=}3 early presses; 9 of 9 in the selection of the table), so one pause alone reads as about one repetition; on Pick all 5 do too, below the count the rule requires. Success falls from 42 to 27 and from 47 to 25 (p=.001p{=}.001 and p<10−5p<10^{-5}). On Swing the clock and skip-one accounts agree here (Tab. 21), so this cell measures the size of the effect, not which account holds. A second pause adds failures (Pick 27 to 21, p=.15p{=}.15; Swing 25 to 14, p=.03p{=}.03), and on Swing makes the press more frequent (10 to 17 of the 23 episodes with K=3K{=}3), but not earlier (all 17 after two swings). With 2×3002{\times}300 pauses on test episodes its few K=3K{=}3 early presses split on Pick (4 after one repetition, 3 after two; n=7n{=}7) and lean to one swing on Swing (4 of 5). That Swing run was pre-registered (length-independent if ≥\geq75% of K=3K{=}3 early presses come after two swings, duration-carrying if ≥\geq75% after one, no verdict below n=8n{=}8); with n=5n{=}5 it gives no verdict. We repeated it on the held-out episodes, Pick and Swing, with the same rule. All early presses with K=3K{=}3: Pick n=13n{=}13, 7 after two and 6 after one; Swing n=9n{=}9, 6 after two, 2 after one, 1 before the first. Neither reaches 75%, so the outcome is open on both tasks, with enough presses this time (in the selection of the table, 6 of 12 and 4 of 7 after two). Success falls from 46 to 16 and from 46 to 19 (p<10−7p<10^{-7} both); Clock on the same episodes presses after one in 29 of 29 with K≥3K{\geq}3. What does change with length is the kind of failure, not the success rate (Pick 21 at 2×1002{\times}100, 22 at 2×3002{\times}300; Swing 14 and 13): on Swing, early presses fall from 26 to 16 of the failures and other failures rise from 10 to 21, whereas Clock stays early (37 of 40 failures at 2×1002{\times}100, 38 of 44 at 2×3002{\times}300). Whether NoClock reads the length of a pause is thus open: on test episodes longer pauses add no early presses, and at 2×3002{\times}300 a part of the presses, not all as with Clock, comes one repetition sooner than at 2×1002{\times}100. A plausible reading of that part, not tested, is that at 2×3002{\times}300 the null frames take most of the 32 slots and crowd out the frames of completed swings. The explicit clock, by contrast, carries the duration. A pre-registered prediction that NoClock’s press ratio falls with the length of the null interval missed (0.60 at two virtual 100-step pauses, 0.71 at 300); it was tested with the real frames of the visible pause packed against slot 31 and the null slots left empty, a left-padded layout never seen in training.

F.5 Linear probe of the memory tokens

A linear probe tests whether elapsed time or progress can be read from NoClock’s memory tokens, and whether a pause inflates the reading. Design: Clock and NoClock; training demonstrations of both tasks, one sample every 10 steps from step 64; memory of 32 frames uniform over [0,s][0,s], encoded by each model’s own memory encoder and averaged per slot. Features: slot features in slot order (PCA to 32 dimensions per slot), or their mean and s.d. over slots. Targets: elapsed steps, repetitions completed; ridge regression, 5-fold cross-validation by episode. Pause test: two still 100-frame pauses inserted before execution frames 100 and 250, same working step. Criteria fixed before the first run: time is readable if held-out R2≥0.8R^{2}\geq 0.8 from NoClock’s ordered features; pauses inflate it if NoClock’s predicted elapsed time rises by at least 50% of the 200 null steps and its predicted repetitions by more than 0.3 (Clock is the positive control); otherwise we report only the causal controls.

Result (Tab. 22). Time stays linearly readable without time stamps: NoClock’s ordered features give held-out R2R^{2} 0.92 and 0.89 for elapsed steps (criterion met on both tasks), from the content and slot order of the memory alone. Clock, the positive control, reads all 200 null steps as elapsed time and about 1.3 extra repetitions. For NoClock the pauses push the reading up on both tasks (repetitions +0.94+0.94 and +0.53+0.53, above the 0.3 criterion), but the elapsed-time shift meets the 50% criterion only on PickXtimes (56%); on SwingXtimes it is 27%. By the rule fixed in advance, the pause-inflation criterion is met on PickXtimes and not on SwingXtimes, so we draw no conclusion from the inflation test. Two limits: the repetition target is correlated with elapsed time in demonstrations, so a probe for one partly reads the other; and a linear read-out shows what the memory encodes, not what the action expert uses, which the causal controls above address.

F.6 Number of null slots

Null block (Tab. 19) varies the number of slots that show nothing happening while keeping the time span of the memory and the event times of the visible pause; no pause takes place. It was pre-registered with two outcomes: an occupancy dose (success non-increasing over m=1,3,6m{=}1,3,6 on both tasks, and m=6m{=}6 at least 8 episodes below m=1m{=}1 with McNemar p<.05p<.05 on one task and lower on the other) or a block read as one event (m=1m{=}1 doing at least 75% of the damage of m=6m{=}6 on both tasks, with m=6m{=}6 against m=1m{=}1 not significant on either). Table 23 gives an occupancy dose on both tasks. Two null slots cost nothing; twelve, about as many as a visible 2×1002{\times}100 pause leaves at t=300t{=}300, cost about as much as the pause on PickXtimes (24 against 21) and most of it on SwingXtimes (23 against 14). The failures keep the signature of the visible pause: at m=6m{=}6, 15 of 26 failures on PickXtimes and 23 of 27 on SwingXtimes are early presses, and every early press at K=3K{=}3 comes after two repetitions (7 of 7 and 16 of 16, in episodes that succeed without it), as under the visible pause (14 of 14 on SwingXtimes; Sec. F.4).

F.7 What these controls do not establish

The read-out is only partly identified: null swap rules out the phase shown in the null frames, duplicate fill rules out sparser real history, and null block shows that the damage grows with the number of null slots, but not which property of a block of identical slots NoClock reads. A second training seed of both models repeats the main cells (Appendix A), with a less clean press-count contrast; same-seed retrainings of Clock differ by up to 9 episodes on hidden cells (Tab. 4).

Appendix G Other memory designs and an independent policy

Among RoboMME’s released memories, the way a memory selects its contents predicts what a null event does to it. Two independent policies on other backbones, which both add to memory at every step, fit less neatly; we report them in full.

G.1 SimpleMemVLA

SimpleMemVLA [54] is an independent code base (Qwen3.5-4B with an action head of about 0.9B parameters) that shares only the benchmark with MME-VLA; we evaluate its released RoboMME checkpoint unchanged. It keeps every frame at 2 Hz in a fixed window of 120 frames, each preceded by a textual time stamp. The window is padded at the start with copies of the first frame, so the stamps always read 0.2 to 59.2 s; elapsed time is visible only as how many slots hold real frames. On PickXtimes (Tab. 24), history resampling, the analogue of rescaling the time stamps of FrameSamp, spreads the real history over round⁡(n​s)\mathrm{round}(ns) slots (frames repeated for s=1.5s{=}1.5, skipped for s=0.5s{=}0.5; stamps and current frame unchanged). Text-stamp rescaling multiplies the stamps by ss, which moves the current frame’s stamp to values never seen in training; we treat it as exploratory.

Resampling the history shifts the failure; rescaling the stamps does not.

A history that looks 1.5 times longer causes only early stops, and one that looks half as long mostly extra repetitions, with the same counts on test and on held-out validation episodes. Almost all of these failures fall among the 6 episodes per split with K=5K{=}5 (×1.5\times 1.5: 6 of 6 on both splits; ×0.5\times 0.5: 5 of 6 on test, 4 of 6 on validation); no episode with K≤4K\leq 4 fails on test. The cells are individually weak (p=.031p{=}.031 and .063.063 on test, .13.13 and .22.22 on validation), and the ×1.5\times 1.5 failures occur when the resampled history fills 98 to 119 of the 120 slots, more than any unperturbed PickXtimes episode does (at most about 88), so part of this effect may be out of distribution. Rescaling the text stamps barely matters (49 and 47); the three failures at ×0.5\times 0.5 are early stops, opposite to the clock prediction, at stamps outside the training range, and we do not interpret them.

Null events on PickXtimes: fidgets hurt, pauses barely do.

Two 5-second pauses add about 20 frames to a window that our episodes never fill and cost 3 episodes against the hidden condition (47 against 50, p=.25p{=}.25); we had predicted a loss of at least 5, so this prediction failed. Fidgets of the same duration cost 12 (38 against 50, p<10−3p<10^{-3}), mostly early stops, spread over all KK rather than confined to K=5K{=}5. We did not run 15-second pauses: 60 additional frames would push some episodes toward the end of the window and mix truncation into the comparison.

SwingXtimes (pre-registered).

We repeated the null-event and history-resampling cells on SwingXtimes (Tab. 25), with predictions written before any result: fidgets visible ≤\leq hidden −6-6 with mostly early failures (P1); pauses less harmful than fidgets (P2); history ×1.5\times 1.5 mostly early and ×0.5\times 0.5 mostly extra failures (P3). P1 holds: fidgets cost 16 (33 against 49, p<10−4p<10^{-4}), 11 of 17 failures early. The fidget nudges the held cube by more than our validity tolerance in most episodes (37 visible, 34 hidden), but this physical disturbance is identical when the fidget frames are hidden, which costs a single episode; among the 31 episodes nudged in both conditions, 16 succeed with the frames visible and 30 with them hidden. P2 holds, narrowly: pauses cost 12 (36 against 48, p=.002p{=}.002), 11 of 14 failures early, unlike on PickXtimes. P3 holds only in part: history ×0.5\times 0.5 costs 7 (42 against 49, p=.04p{=}.04), mostly through extra swings, but ×1.5\times 1.5 costs nothing (50). SimpleMemVLA’s own spoken sub-goal often runs ahead of the environment’s after a fidget (e.g. announcing the second swing while the first is unfinished), so its errors are visible in its language output as well.

G.2 LTM-π\pi

LTM-π\pi [45] is a second independent code base (a modified OpenPI π0.5\pi_{0.5} with a frozen latent-action model). For every pair of consecutive frames it appends one memory token, a projection of the latent transition between them, with ordinal positions and no explicit time stamp. It reports 100 of 100 on PickXtimes and SwingXtimes. We evaluate the released checkpoint (trained on ten times the RoboMME demonstrations) unchanged, through its own server, with our injection client. Deviations from its own evaluator: CPU rendering (as for all our runs), noise seed 7, pauses after policy steps 50 and 160 (it replans every 10 steps), no retry on error. The client checks that each visible frame adds one token, a visible event 100, and a hidden event none.

Predictions fixed before the run (gate: no-event success ≥45\geq 45 on both tasks). If LTM-π\pi reads its memory length, visible pauses should cost at least 6 against hidden ones. If it counts motion, as its tokens suggest, pauses should cost at most 3 and fidgets at least 6. We expected the second.

The gate passes (50 and 50). The motion account fails: visible pauses cost LTM-π\pi as much as fidgets do, almost always through early presses, and on PickXtimes hiding either event leaves success at 50. A still interval is not empty for this memory: it adds one token per step, each encoding a near-zero transition, and the policy reads the extra tokens as progress. On SwingXtimes, hiding the events does not restore success fully (31 and 32): the hidden failures are all extra swings, on nearly the same episodes for pause and fidget, the opposite error to the visible one. Keeping the hold frames until the arm is still does not close this gap (34; Sec. B.1), so the SwingXtimes comparisons above are against no event; visible remains below hidden (p<10−4p<10^{-4} for both events).

G.3 Full numbers for the comparison of memory designs

Table 27 gives the cells behind Tab. 2, with hidden references where they exist, paired pp values, and the two released TokenDrop variants not shown in the main text. K≥2K{\geq}2 counts successes without an event among episodes with at least two repetitions, the only ones in which counting requires memory.

Which “unaffected” rows are informative.

TTT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeed in nearly every episode with K=1K{=}1 (31 of 31 and 30 of 31) but in almost none with K≥2K\geq 2 (9 of 69 and 3 of 69), so their indifference to null events says nothing about their memory; the same holds for text sub-goals on SwingXtimes (1 of 50). The text sub-goals are predicted online by RoboMME’s released Qwen-VL sub-goal model from the current frame, the demonstration video and the sub-goals logged so far (no oracle sub-goals). The informative rows are MemER-style keyframes and text sub-goals on PickXtimes, which solve most episodes with K≥2K\geq 2 (22 and 30 of 34, against 31 for FrameSamp-Modul) and are unchanged by pauses (39 and 48) and by fidgets (38 and 47). Under one-way air-grasps MemER drops from 38 to 27, against 39 when the air-grasps are hidden (−16/+4-16/{+4}, p=.012p{=}.012); text sub-goals are unaffected (44 against 45 hidden).

TokenDrop.

Pauses cost TokenDrop less than FrameSamp but still significantly on PickXtimes (30 against 40 hidden, −12/+2-12/{+2}, p=.013p{=}.013). Fidgets pass the pixel filter and cost far more than pauses: 21 against 42 hidden on PickXtimes (p<10−6p<10^{-6}) and 11 against 36 on SwingXtimes (p<10−7p<10^{-7}). On SwingXtimes the hidden fidget itself costs 9 episodes (36 against 45, p=.022p{=}.022); comparing against the hidden condition removes this physical part. Rescaling TokenDrop’s time stamps (Tab. 13) shifts the failures in the same directions as for FrameSamp, but the drop in success is not significant, and two no-event runs on validation episodes differ by 5 successes, so we treat its clock evidence as exploratory.

Appendix H Data-level fixes

None of the augmentations we tested fixes the failure. Pause augmentation removes the pause damage on PickXtimes only by lowering success without events, a weaker dose keeps more counting but helps no more under pauses, and the earlier augmentations become indifferent to null events because they no longer count.

All models in this section are trained from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} base checkpoint with the recipe of Clock (same data, 30k steps, batch 64, clock on), changing only what the memory sees during training, and are evaluated on the same 50 paired episodes as Clock. Earlier training arms are not reported: an implementation error left their data modifications inactive (applied in the main process but not in the data-loader workers). After the fix, the modified loader reproduces the original samples with all modifications off (60 of 60) and changes the memory inputs with them on (16 of 16).

H.1 Pause-only augmentation

Design.

On 80% of training samples we insert 1–3 synthetic pauses of 20–600 steps into the memory timeline by repeating a frame, with the time stamps advancing as in a real pause; nothing else changes (no replayed segments, no time warp). A held frame is a faithful pause, so if the damage were merely an unseen input, this model should become indifferent to pauses.

Pre-registered decision rules

(written before any result).

  • •

    Pauses fixed: pause 100 ≥\geq own hidden − 6-\,6 and no event ≥\geq Clock − 6-\,6 (PickXtimes ≥35\geq 35, SwingXtimes ≥42\geq 42). Not fixed: pause 100 within ±8\pm 8 of Clock (17 / 10). Otherwise partial.

  • •

    Moving nulls (predicted not fixed): PickXtimes fidget ≤24\leq 24 not fixed, ≥\geq own hidden − 6-\,6 fixed; SwingXtimes fidget ≤18\leq 18 not fixed, same upper rule; SwingXtimes air-grasp-ret ≤21\leq 21 not fixed, ≥35\geq 35 fixed.

  • •

    Clock: ×1.5\times 1.5 ≥\geq own no event − 6-\,6: clock dependence removed; ≤27\leq 27: still reads the clock. ×0.5\times 0.5 ≤\leq own no event − 10-\,10 with mostly extra repetitions: still reads the clock.

  • •

    Route: time only ≤\leq own no event − 10-\,10: the stamp route is still used; ≥\geq own no event − 6-\,6: removed. Content only: no rule, reported descriptively.

Second machine and its control.

The pause-only model was trained and evaluated on a second machine, with the recipe of Clock except FSDP on 2 instead of 4 GPUs; evaluation parity with the cluster is in Appendix A. To separate the machine from the augmentation we retrained Clock there without augmentation (rule written before that training: no-event success at least 35 and 42 excludes the machine, within 6 of the pause-only model implicates it). SwingXtimes passes (46). PickXtimes on the test split falls between the two (32), so we ran held-out episodes on both models, again with the rules written first (control at least 32; pause-only at least 6 below it with p<.05p<.05). Both were met: 45 against 17 (−29/+1-29/{+}1, p<10−6p<10^{-6}), and on SwingXtimes 44 against 20 (−24/+0-24/{+}0, p<10−6p<10^{-6}). All comparisons below are therefore with the retrain on the same machine. The retrain also reproduces the pause damage in a new training on a new machine: 32 to 16 and 46 to 11 under visible pauses, with hidden pauses at 35 and 40. Its difference from Clock on PickXtimes without events goes both ways (−9-9 on test, +7+7 on held-out episodes; Tab. 28), so comparisons between trainings on this cell carry that uncertainty.

Result.

By the rules the pauses are not fixed. The no-event clause fails on both tasks: 24 and 19, against 35 and 42, and also against the retrain. Pause 100 is not fixed on SwingXtimes (10; control 11). On PickXtimes it is at the upper edge of the rule against Clock (25 against 17 ±\pm 8) and just outside it against the retrain (25 against 16, −0/+9-0/{+}9, p=.004p{=}.004), which we count as partial: the pause no longer costs anything (25 against its own 24), at a lower level. On SwingXtimes visible pauses still cost it episodes (19 to 10, −10/+1-10/{+}1, p=.012p{=}.012), including at K=1K{=}1 (9 of 15). The air-grasp is not fixed (17). The stamp route is removed (time only 24 against its own 24, −3/+3-3/{+}3); the ×0.5\times 0.5 rule for still reading the clock is not triggered (21). Three cells meet both conditions of their rule, because the rules assumed that no-event success would hold: ×1.5\times 1.5 (24), PickXtimes fidget (21) and SwingXtimes fidget (14). We give no verdict on them; against the model’s own no-event cell they are −6/+6-6/{+}6, −6/+3-6/{+}3 and −5/+0-5/{+}0, none significant. The loss is in counting: K=1K{=}1 is untouched (Tab. 29, test split), and on held-out episodes K≥2K{\geq}2 falls from 35 to 7 of 40 and from 25 to 1 of 31. On the test split, the same fall is 31 to 4 of 35 on SwingXtimes and 16 to 8 of 34 on PickXtimes (−12/+4-12/{+}4, p=.077p{=}.077, not significant).

A weaker dose.

This model adds about 270 steps of pause per sample on average. To test whether the strength alone causes the loss, we trained a weaker dose on the same machine with the same seed: pauses on 30% of samples, at most 2, of 20–100 steps (about 22 null steps per sample), no noise. Rules, written before training, against the retrain: counting kept if no-event success is at least 26 and 40 on test and at least 39 and 38 on held-out episodes; pauses improved if pause 100 is at least 25 and 20 and within 6 of its own hidden cell. Both kept: a weaker dose works for pauses. Counting kept only: it keeps counting but does not help under pauses. Counting not kept: the cost is not only a matter of strength. SwingXtimes keeps counting (48 on test, 45 held-out; K≥2K{\geq}2 held-out 27 of 31, retrain 25) and pauses do not improve (12 against 20; its own hidden 43): it keeps counting but does not help under pauses. PickXtimes does not keep counting on held-out episodes (31 against 39; retrain 45, −15/+1-15/{+}1, p<10−3p<10^{-3}; K≥2K{\geq}2 21 of 40, retrain 35, strong dose 7), although on test it is above the retrain (39 against 32), and pauses do not improve (19 against 25; its own hidden 34). By the rule, on PickXtimes the counting cost is not only a matter of strength; it is smaller at the weaker dose, and the gap to Clock on the cluster (38 held-out, −10/+3-10/{+}3, p=.09p{=}.09) is within the spread between trainings on this cell. The weaker dose also leaves the clock read: time stamps ×1.5\times 1.5 lower success from 39 to 30 (−12/+3-12/{+}3, p=.035p{=}.035; 19 of 20 failures early). At neither strength does pause augmentation move the pause damage.

H.2 Augmentation with replayed segments, and training on event-indexed timelines

Three earlier training interventions were run after the fix: paug adds to the pauses, on 50% of samples, a replayed segment (the most recent 15–60 frames inserted reversed and then forward, so the robot appears to go out and come back); saug2 adds to paug a time warp of the history (0.5–2×\times, log-uniform) on 80% of samples; eim2 is trained on memories passed through the simulator-contact event index of Appendix I.

They are indifferent to null events because they no longer count.

saug2 and paug are flat across all their cells (PickXtimes 20–27, SwingXtimes 11–22): pauses, fidgets, air-grasps and even ×1.5\times 1.5 (24 and 23) no longer hurt, and within each model no null-event cell differs significantly from its own no-event cell. But their no-event success falls far below Clock: PickXtimes 25 and 22 against 41 (−16/+0-16/{+}0, −19/+0-19/{+}0), SwingXtimes 17 and 16 against 48 (−31/+0-31/{+}0, −32/+0-32/{+}0), all p<10−4p<10^{-4}. Table 29 shows why: K=1K{=}1 is intact, K≥2K\geq 2 almost always fails (on SwingXtimes, 23 of 33 saug2 failures occur during the swing itself, which we attribute to the time warp). eim2 counts better; its 9-episode gap on PickXtimes without any null event (32 against 41, −11/+2-11/{+}2, p=.022p{=}.022, all at K≥3K\geq 3) is within what an unaugmented retrain on a second machine also shows on this cell (Sec. H.1), so we do not read it as a cost. paug and saug2 therefore cannot serve as a fix, and eim2 shows no gain under null events. We first attributed the loss in paug and saug2 to the replayed segment, which copies recorded frames, objects included, so that in memory it looks like a real repetition that the label says does not count. The pause-only model has no replayed segments and loses counting too (Sec. H.1), so the segment is not necessary for this loss, though it remains unusable as a moving null event for the same reason. This holds for any moving null synthesised from recorded demonstrations, the only option on real-robot data (a simulator could render true moving nulls, which we did not do). Applied to demonstrations, the event index in turn collapses real repetitions (116 of 191 PickXtimes loops cross a sub-goal change, Tab. 33), so eim2 learns to count from memories with repetitions missing. Because both augmentations contain replayed segments, they do not test whether faithful pause augmentation alone removes the pause damage; the pause-only model does.

Appendix I The event index

The event index of Sec. 6 is a test-time intervention that removes null frames from a time-indexed memory, to test the diagnosis rather than to propose a general null-event detector. Table 30 gives the full numbers behind Fig. 8.

I.1 Definition

The detector processes the policy’s execution frames online and maintains a kept sequence; only kept frames enter memory, and their time positions are their indices in the kept sequence, so the memory clock advances only with kept frames. A frame is a barrier if the scene outside the robot changed with respect to the last kept frame, or if a grip or load switch (Sec. I.2) occurred; a barrier is always kept and no stretch is collapsed across it. Between barriers, two rules apply:

  • •

    Loop closure. If the robot configuration returns to within tolerance of a kept frame pp after having left it by more than the exit distance, and the scene outside the robot equals that at pp, the kept frames after pp are collapsed to one frame (the kept frame farthest from pp) and one clock tick.

  • •

    Stillness. If the configuration stays within the stillness tolerance of the frame at which a stop began and the scene is unchanged, the first 5 frames of the stop are kept (grace) and later ones are dropped.

All tolerances (Tab. 31) were set during development on test-split episodes and then frozen, identical for all 16 RoboMME tasks and all models; the held-out replication (Sec. I.4) used environment seeds never used in development.

I.2 Signals and how they are obtained

The decision uses four signals, none of which is the simulator’s object state.

  • •

    Robot joint configuration (7 arm joints, 2 finger joints): proprioception, available on any arm.

  • •

    Robot silhouette in the front camera, used only to ignore the robot’s own pixels when testing whether the scene changed. In all experiments it is the simulator’s segmentation of the robot links. On a robot it can be rendered from the joint readings and the camera calibration; we did not implement this rendering.

  • •

    Gripper width. The gripper is holding while the width has settled strictly between closed-on-nothing and open; a switch of this state (a grasp or a release) is an event. An air-grasp closes to empty and never holds.

  • •

    Net external force on the arm: in all experiments the sum of the simulator’s contact impulses between the robot and anything else, with the robot links merged so that grip forces cancel. This is the quantity a wrist force/torque sensor measures; we did not model sensor noise. A switch between loaded and unloaded (lift-off, set-down, press, push) is an event.

The simulator-contact variant replaces the last two signals by the simulator’s list of contact pairs. Both variants use the simulator segmentation and noise-free renders; the 5-pixel scene tolerance would have to be revisited for a real camera.

I.3 What the detector collapses

Recall on injected null intervals.

Table 32 gives the fraction of injected null frames that the detector removes. Pauses are removed almost entirely; the missed frames are the deceleration at the start of each pause and the 5 grace frames. A one-way air-grasp ends elsewhere, so its descent and approach never close a loop, and only about half of it is removed. For returning events the closure is all-or-nothing: in 4 of the episodes lost on SwingXtimes air-grasp-ret, the return stopped 1.3–3 units short of the starting configuration and the whole excursion (≈\approx110 frames) was kept. On the Clock model, each 100-step pause on SwingXtimes leaves about 11 frames (recall ≈\approx0.87).

The policy’s own loops.

PickXtimes is the only task in which the policy makes many loops of its own: after releasing a cube it lifts and comes back down to it (26.6 loop closures per episode without null events; 23.9% of frames collapsed, against 0.6% on BinFill).

Demonstration-replay audit.

Replayed on the RoboMME training demonstrations (Tab. 33), the detector collapses 19.0% of PickXtimes frames, and 116 of 191 closed loops have ends carrying different recorded sub-goals, almost all “place the cube onto the target” →\to “pick up the cube for the second time”: a real repetition returns the robot and the scene to a state they were in before. VideoRepick shows the same pattern (25.6%, 144 of 205). These two tasks are where an event index can fail by construction (Sec. I.6).

I.4 Effect on the released policies

Table 34 gives the full probe grid on the released FrameSamp-Modul policy (simulator-contact variant) with the hidden reference and two appearance-based baselines: g0, which drops every frame in which neither the robot state nor the image changes (no grace) without advancing the clock over them, and TokenDrop, the released memory that selects tokens by pixel change.

Dropping still frames (g0) recovers pauses as well as the event index does, or better (PickXtimes pause: 42 against 34), but recovers nothing under fidgets or a returning air-grasp, which change pixels without changing the world: the same dissociation as TokenDrop in Tab. 2.

Other released variants.

The same detector, unchanged, raises FrameSamp-Context under pause 300 from 11 to 27 (PickXtimes) and from 10 to 28 (SwingXtimes), and FrameSamp-Expert from 14 to 35 and from 11 to 34 (Expert hidden, PickXtimes: 45); its cost without null events on both is in Tab. 36.

I.5 Non-privileged versus simulator-contact signals

Replayed on 12 demonstrations of each of the 16 tasks, the non-privileged variant misses at most 2 frames per task that the simulator-contact variant collapses. It collapses more in six tasks (BinFill +102 frames, +20%; VideoRepick +71; SwingXtimes +45; ButtonUnmaskSwap +17; PickHighlight +14; ButtonUnmask +12; the other 10 tasks 0), because gripper width and net force miss some contact changes (event recall BinFill 0.80, ButtonUnmask 0.51, VideoUnmask 0.29, precision ≈\approx1). Table 35 tests whether this over-collapse costs success: none of the 12 compared cells differs significantly. On Clock the two variants also agree: non-privileged / simulator-contact PickXtimes no event 36 / 36, pause 34 / 33, fidget 33 / 31; SwingXtimes no event 48 / 46, pause 30 / 26, air-grasp-ret 43 / 42 (not tested pairwise). On held-out episodes (pre-registered: a gain of at least 8 with McNemar p<.05p<.05 on each task, tolerances unchanged), the non-privileged variant on Clock raises PickXtimes under pauses from 10 to 36 (−0/+26-0/{+}26, p<10−7p<10^{-7}; no event 38) and SwingXtimes from 14 to 32 (−1/+19-1/{+}19, p<10−4p<10^{-4}; no event 44); early presses fall from 40 to 9 and from 30 to 15 of the failures. These comparisons establish that the decision does not depend on the simulator’s contact list, not that the detector is deployable: the silhouette and the force are simulator stand-ins (Sec. I.2).

I.6 Costs, residual gap and boundaries

Cost without null events.

On PickXtimes (Tab. 36) the cost was first observed on the test split; a held-out replication was then pre-registered (a net loss with episode-aggregated p<.05p<.05, three policy seeds) and confirmed: 139 to 120 of 150 (17 episodes worse, 4 better; sign-flip permutation p=.005p{=}.005). Under a Holm correction over our 59-test family neither split survives alone (pHolm=.10p_{\text{Holm}}=.10 test, .15.15 val); the pooled test+val comparison does (31 worse, 6 better, pHolm=.001p_{\text{Holm}}=.001). With the event index the policy performs an extra repetition, which the stock policy never does (stock 0 of 250 episodes, event index 32 of 300 over test and val; val alone 0 against 18 of 150): collapsing the loop back to a released cube gives the policy back the memory that made it leave, so it repeats the step. Across the other 15 tasks (SwingXtimes included; without it 272 against 269 of 700) the event index costs nothing overall (316 against 317 of 750, −22/+23-22/{+}23, p=1.0p{=}1.0; a 95% interval of about ±1.8\pm 1.8 points on the net).

Residual gap to the hidden reference.

On the 7 test probes the event index stays 47 episodes below the hidden reference (248 against 295 of 350). Table 37 attributes each of the 47 from the detector’s per-frame log, paired with the same episode under the hidden condition (rules hard-coded in the analysis script; counts are net of chance expectation and of reverse pairs, so approximate). About a quarter of the gap is false collapse, entirely on PickXtimes and in the same episodes that carry the clean-episode cost; about an eighth is the one-way boundary; slightly more than a quarter is missed null frames; the rest is within run-to-run noise. We did not tune the detector to close this gap.

Randomised micro-stops.

Brief stops at random action-chunk boundaries (probability 0.3 per boundary, 5–40 steps each, until a 300-step budget; on average 7.2 stops and ≈\approx157 steps per episode; same schedule in every condition of an episode) harm through memory nearly as much as long pauses: hiding their frames restores success (Tab. 38). The event index recovers little and not significantly. Each stop begins with a deceleration and settling phase that is neither still nor a closed loop, and the event index keeps the first 5 frames of every stop by design (the grace); summed over many short stops, it keeps 35–50% of the stop frames (66–71 per episode) and g0 36–39% (55–60), whereas the hidden condition keeps none. This form of null event, the one a deployed robot is most likely to produce, is not solved here.

Summary of the boundaries.

The event index removes the damage of null events that return the world to a previous state; it partly fails on null events that do not return (one-way air-grasp, randomised micro-stops); it can fail where a real repetition also returns the world to a previous state (PickXtimes, and in demonstrations VideoRepick); and it is wrong by construction where elapsed time is the task (TimedTransfer, Appendix J). These limits follow from a state-return criterion, though we observed them before explaining them, and the miss on micro-stops owes as much to the detector’s mechanics.

Appendix J An exploratory study on MIKASA-Robo

Summary.

On MIKASA-Robo [8] we trained the same architecture (64 memory slots) from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} base checkpoint on BlinkCount, in which a light blinks KK times and the robot must then press a button KK times and submit. The policy solves only 24 of 50 episodes, below the competence level we set in advance, so this evidence is exploratory. In the demonstrations the cue lasts longer the more blinks it contains, with non-overlapping ranges, so the time at which the cue ends identifies KK. This is consistent with reading the cue’s duration: with the cue fixed to 50 steps for every KK, success falls from 24 to 6, and almost all remaining successes are for the one count whose usual cue lasts about that long (K=5K{=}5: 5 of 9; other KK: 1 of 41); seeing the light does not help (9 with the light hidden as well). Faster time stamps make it over-press (38 of 42 failures), and a visible pause after the cue reduces success to 8, against 23 when hidden, here through the stored frames rather than the stamps.

Model and data.

We trained FrameSamp-Modul (clock on, 64 memory slots) from the π0.5\pi_{0.5} base checkpoint with the recipe of Clock (30k steps, batch 64) on 1250 MIKASA-Robo demonstrations (about 183k frames) of BlinkCount (Medium and Hard) and TimedTransfer (Easy, Medium and Hard), and evaluate BlinkCount-Medium (K≤5K\leq 5) and TimedTransfer-Medium. With 32 slots, uniform time sampling loses blinks (3 steps each): replayed on the real episode lengths, blinks remain countable at the last step in 54% of Medium episodes, against 100% with 64. The loader does not use the hook affected by the error of Appendix H.

Task structure.

In BlinkCount-Medium the cue lasts a waiting time of 5–10 steps plus KK blinks of 3 steps separated by 3–5 dark steps, and ends when a phase light turns green. The step at which the cue ends identifies KK: the ranges do not overlap (K=1K{=}1: 12–18, K=2K{=}2: 20–23, K=3K{=}3: 25–31, K=4K{=}4: 32–38, K=5K{=}5: 39–47). The robot must then press a button KK times and submit. Failures are over-press (a (K+1)(K{+}1)-th press, which ends the episode), early submit, or timeout. In TimedTransfer the robot must move an object while a timer light is in its target window, so reading time is correct.

Pre-registered gate.

Before any result we required, for interpreting any other cell, BlinkCount no-event success ≥60%\geq 60\% and ≥30\geq 30 points above an uninformative control (blank cue: blink light hidden throughout), and TimedTransfer no-event success ≥50%\geq 50\%. The gate failed: BlinkCount reached 48% (24/50), and the blank cue gave 23. The blank cue is informative, since its duration still identifies KK; against a cue padded to 50 steps with the light hidden, the margin is 30 points (24 against 9, +8/−23+8/{-}23, p=.011p{=}.011), but the first criterion is still not met. A retraining with cue duration decoupled from KK was pre-registered to repair the gate but never run. All MIKASA results are therefore exploratory; each cell added after the gate had a written prediction before it was run.

TimedTransfer, the positive control.

Without events the policy succeeds in all 50 TimedTransfer-Medium episodes. Rescaling the stamps fails every episode in the predicted direction: ×1.5\times 1.5 gives 0 (all 50 too early), ×0.5\times 0.5 gives 0 (all 50 late). A 50-step pause at step 40 gives 35 when visible (15 late, +0/−15+0/{-}15, p<.001p{<}.001) and 0 when hidden (all 50 late): hiding a pause removes real elapsed time from memory, so this failure holds by construction.

Reading.

  • •

    KK is read from the cue duration. With the cue fixed to 50 steps, success concentrates on K=5K{=}5, whose natural cue end (39–47) is closest to 50 (5 of 9, against 1 of 41 for other KK), and failures are over-presses (36). Hiding the light as well gives a similar result (9), though it changes which KK succeed (K=4K{=}4: 0/16 visible, 7/16 hidden; K=5K{=}5: 5/9 and 2/9).

  • •

    The duration is read from the time stamps. Rescaled from step 0, they shift the inferred count both ways: over-presses rise from 15 to 38 at ×1.5\times 1.5 (p<.001p{<}.001); early submissions rise from 11 to 19 at ×0.67\times 0.67, with no significant change in success (p=.33p{=}.33) because the shift also corrects over-counted episodes (K=3,4K{=}3,4 improve, K=1,2,5K{=}1,2,5 drop).

  • •

    Pre-registered miss (H1). We predicted that stamps rescaled after the cue would cause early submissions at ×1.5\times 1.5 and extra presses at ×0.5\times 0.5. Instead, ×1.5\times 1.5 from step 50 costs 9 episodes (p=.049p{=}.049) through over-presses, and ×0.5\times 0.5 has no effect (26, p=.80p{=}.80).

  • •

    The pause acts through memory content. The pre-registered hypothesis H2 (visible pause ≥10\geq 10 points below no event with mostly early submissions, hidden within 6) held: a visible pause after the first press causes early submissions (41 of 42 failures), a hidden one does not (23). Under pre-registered split thresholds (≤14\leq 14 with mostly early submissions: route used; ≥18\geq 18: not used), content only reproduces the damage (5, 42 early) and time only does not (19, mostly over-presses), as for NoClock (Sec. 5.3).

Run-to-run noise: a duplicate no-event evaluation differs from no event by +7/−4+7/{-}4.

What MIKASA does and does not show.

On a second benchmark, with a different action space and demonstration source, a time-indexed memory reads a task variable (KK) from time when time predicts it in the demonstrations, and the stamp manipulation acts on time (TimedTransfer). It does not show that a competent BlinkCount policy is vulnerable: base success is 48%, the gate failed, and the decoupled retraining was not run.

Appendix K Pre-registered predictions and their outcomes

For the key tests we recorded the prediction and the decision rule, including thresholds, in a dated log before the run. Below are the predictions that bear on main-text claims, with their outcomes, including those that missed.

  • •

    NoClock (registered before training): manipulation check, rescaling its (absent) stamps changes nothing (44 against 42, met); pauses still hurt by at least 8 episodes on PickXtimes (21 against 42, met), with mostly early failures (21 of 29, met).

  • •

    SimpleMemVLA: history stretched 1.5 times adds at least 5 early stops and compressed 0.5 times adds at least 3 extra repetitions (met on test and on validation episodes); visible pauses cost at least 5 episodes against hidden (not met: 47 against 50); visible fidgets do (met: 38 against 50).

  • •

  • •

    Event index, held-out replication on new environment seeds: gains on the seven probes (met in 6 of 7; the one-way air-grasp was not significant); on Clock under pauses, a gain of at least 8 on each task (met: 10 to 36, 14 to 32).

  • •

    Pause-only augmentation (Sec. H.1): pauses fixed with no-event success kept (not met on either task); second-machine control and held-out comparison, rules written before each run (met, PickXtimes only on held-out episodes). Weaker dose: counting kept (met on SwingXtimes, not on PickXtimes held-out, 31, below the threshold of 39; retrain 45); pauses improved (not met on either task).

  • •

    MIKASA route split: if the stamp route carried the pause effect, time only would fall below 18 (it did not: 19); content only reproduced the effect (5).

    MIKASA: the pre-registered gate that the policy reads the light failed (Appendix J).

    Linear probe of the memory tokens (Sec. F.5): time readable from NoClock (met on both tasks); pause inflation met on PickXtimes, not on SwingXtimes (elapsed shift 27% against 50%).

    Null-slot dose on NoClock (Sec. F.6): occupancy dose rather than one block read as one event (met on both tasks: m=6m{=}6 against m=1m{=}1, −21-21 and −24-24).

  • •

    Second training seed of Clock and NoClock (Appendix A): five rules, all met.

  • •

    One pause on NoClock (Sec. F.4): one 5-second pause alone reads as about one repetition (met: 10 of 10 early presses after two swings at K=3K{=}3, SwingXtimes). 2×3002{\times}300 on held-out episodes, length-independent or duration-carrying: neither met on either task (7 of 13 and 6 of 9 after two repetitions); open.

Appendix L Every cell of the main text

Tables 41, 42, 43 and 44 list every cell of the four models analysed throughout, one per model; other designs and tasks are in their own sections. They give Wilson 95% intervals, paired changes, exact McNemar pp-values with Holm correction over the 42 comparisons, and failure classes (Appendix A); Tab. 40 splits the same cells by KK.

Success by KK.

On PickXtimes, episodes with K=1K=1 are almost untouched by pauses and fidgets in every model (16 of 16 under pauses), where there is no decision to stop early; on SwingXtimes pauses do cost some K=1K=1 episodes (10, 10 and 9 of 15 for the released model, Clock and NoClock), for reasons we have not resolved. For K≥2K\geq 2 success collapses (released model, PickXtimes: 0 of 34 under pauses). The PickXtimes air-grasp cell does not follow this pattern (2 of 16 at K=1K=1): the returning gripper often re-grasps the cube it has just released, so the event is not null for this task, and we do not use the cell (Appendix B).
